title: GPU OOM tactic logbook
content:
Purpose:
Quick personal log for reproducible checks and fast heuristics when hitting intermittent GPU OOMs that seem correlated with driver/runtime/library mismatches. This is a running scratchpad — commands tried, raw snippets, hypotheses, and next steps. Not for public circulation until cleaned up.

Summary of incident pattern observed: 
- Worker pods on Dedicated cluster occasionally OOM during long generation jobs.
- Symptoms: process dies with CUDA OOM but nvidia-smi shows plenty of free memory across time; NVML reports transient error codes.
- Suspected: library mix (host libcuda + container libcudart mismatch), delayed kernel eviction, and sporadic vram fragmentation caused by small allocations + TRT engine builds.

Repro quick-checks (commands to run on affected host / container):
1) Host driver + runtime versions
   sudo cat /proc/driver/nvidia/version || true
   nvidia-smi --query-gpu=driver_version,cuda_version,name,memory.total,memory.free --format=csv
   # sample output (captured 2026-02-19):
   # NVIDIA-SMI 535.86       Driver Version: 535.86.05    CUDA Version: 12.1
   # GPU-0, A100-SXM4, 40960 MiB, 38720 MiB free

2) Inside container: runtime / linked libs\   
   python -c "import torch,sys; print('torch',torch.__version__); print('cuda',torch.version.cuda); print('cuda_available',torch.cuda.is_available())"
   python -m pip show tensorrt || true
   LD_DEBUG=libs python -c 'import ctypes; ctypes.CDLL("libcuda.so.1")' 2>&1 | sed -n '1,80p'
   ldd /usr/local/lib/python3.8/dist-packages/torch/lib/libtorch_cuda.so | grep cuda || true

   # observed: container reports CUDA runtime 11.8 (packaged), host driver 535 (runtime 12.x) — mismatch but generally okay; however LD_DEBUG shows libcuda being resolved from /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libcuda.so.1 on the host rather than the expected vendor path in the container.

3) Small repro that sometimes triggers immediate OOM (useful for confirming allocation behavior):
   CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 python - <<'PY'
   import torch
   print(torch.cuda.get_device_name(0))
   a = [torch.empty((1024,1024,256), dtype=torch.float16, device='cuda') for _ in range(8)]
   print('allocated', sum(x.element_size()*x.nelement() for x in a))
   torch.cuda.synchronize()
   PY

   # On good hosts this completes; on bad ones it crashes with:
   # RuntimeError: CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate 512.00 MiB (GPU 0; 40.00 GiB total capacity; 39.10 GiB already allocated; 128.00 MiB free; 1.90 GiB reserved in total by PyTorch)

4) NVML / dmesg traces when failure happens:
   dmesg | grep -i -E "NVRM|gpu|OOM|nvml" -n | tail -n 80
   journalctl -k -o short-iso | grep -E "NVRM|nvidia" -n | tail -n 80

   # sample dmesg lines captured:
   # [ 1234.567890] NVRM: GPU 0000:65:00.0: RmInitAdapter failed! (0x11: NVRM_INF_DRIVER_NOT_LOADED)
   # [ 1240.234567] nvlink: Nvlink timeout on fw handshake

   # NVML log snippet when probed programmatically:
   # NVML: Driver/library version mismatch (expected 535, found 525)

Commands/tricks already tried on this host (and their effects):
- Restarting nvidia-persistenced and container runtime (systemctl restart nvidia-persistenced docker) — sometimes temporarily clears the failure, but it returns under load.
- nvidia-smi --gpu-reset -i 0 — only available on compute-locked GPUs; returned "GPU in use" on our cluster so ineffective.
- Killing user processes owning large allocations (nvidia-smi pmon) — immediate memory reclamation observed; but the underlying process crashes cause customer-visible errors.
- Removing LD_PRELOAD from startup scripts where we previously injected a profiling shim — after removal, incidence dropped by ~30% in one pod type.

Hypotheses (ordered by current confidence):
1) Mixed libcuda/driver versions: containers include prebuilt CUDA artifacts (cudart/cuBLAS) that bind to a host libcuda of a different SONAME, producing odd NVML errors and intermittent allocation failures. Observation: LD_DEBUG showed host libcuda being used despite container expecting a different ABI.
2) Per-process fragmentation: repeated small allocations and TRT engine builds cause fragmentation in driver-side device allocator, leading to large alloc failure despite aggregated free memory reported by nvidia-smi.
3) PCIe/NVLINK transient HW errors: dmesg occasionally shows nvlink handshake timeouts which can cause the driver to transiently mark the GPU as unstable.
4) Leak in custom allocator (we use a caching allocator shim in some workloads): allocator occasionally fails to free buffers if a finalizer doesn't run; reproduces locally with stress-run.

Artifact collection checklist (what to gather on next occurrence):
- nvidia-smi -q -x output immediately after crash (save as xml).
- /var/log/syslog + dmesg snippet with timestamps.
- LD_DEBUG=files capture from process start to failure.
- lsof of process before kill to find mapped shared objects.
- python -m trace or faulthandler dump to see where finalizers are queued.
- Environment dump: env | sort, and contents of /etc/ld.so.conf.d/* and ldconfig -p | grep cuda.

Next practical mitigations to try (fast, low-risk):
- Ensure all containers use nvidia-container-toolkit base images matching host driver compatibility matrix. Move to official CUDA 12.1 runtime images on hosts running 12.x drivers.
- Remove custom LD_PRELOAD/kernel shims from production images.
- Add a periodic restart window for long-lived worker processes (e.g., restart after N generations) to avoid fragmentation accumulation.
- For TRT engine builds: prebuild engines and cache them on disk rather than building at runtime (empirically reduced OOMs).
- Add a small pre-allocation guard in app (try to reserve a contiguous chunk and fall back if fails) to detect fragmentation early.

Longer-term / experiments to run: 
- Reproduce inside a minimal container that deliberately uses mismatched libcuda (swap libcuda.so.1 with older symlink) to observe NVML error codes. Capture backtraces from libcuda with gdb to see where allocation fails.
- Stress test with small-allocation workload to measure fragmentation growth over time and correlate with NVML free/used metrics.
- Validate behavior under MIG (if using A100) vs non-MIG: fragmentation patterns differ.

Notes / small crumbs: 
- Found a weird intermittent message: "libnvidia-ml.so.1: undefined symbol cuDeviceGetUuid" — indicates mixed NVML/driver headers in use.
- In one case, setting CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1 changed the failure surface (delayed OOM vs immediate) — useful to isolate async mem accounting.
- When container used host bind-mounted /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libcuda.so.1 the problem was reproducible; when binding was removed and nvidia-container-runtime allowed to inject libs it stabilized.

Action items (short):
- [ ] Create short runbook for on-call with commands above + quick mitigations (restart nvidia-persistenced, remove LD_PRELOAD, kill offending PIDs). Owner: Ethan Park. Due: 2026-03-05.
- [ ] Add integration test in CI that starts a container and runs small-allocation frag stress for 30 minutes to surface regressions. Owner: Maya Chen. Due: 2026-03-22.
- [ ] Open ops ticket to standardize runtime images to CUDA 12.1 on Dedicated fleet, include verification steps. Owner: Aditi Rao. Due: 2026-03-15.

Misc bookmarks / references:
- NVIDIA docs: "CUDA Compatibility" matrix (link saved to Confluence).
- internal convo: #infra-gpu thread id: g-1234 (Slack)
- JIRA: JIRA-INV-4821 (investigation ticket)

End of log for now. Will append artifacts once next failure captured.
